A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAP research. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original pairwise and multi-view registration experiments, ablations, runtime measurements and extensive validation results, including appendix Tables 8–10.

after.justification: v2 reports original registration experiments, cross-domain benchmark comparisons, ablations and offline SLAM results, including Tables 2, 3, 8 and 9.

M1.justification: The explicit global scene-scale embedding in v1's conditioning input is removed in v2 Section 3.4 and Appendix B.2. Canonicalization still uses scale. The core MiniSpinNet descriptors, alternating-attention transformer, flow-matching objective and per-step rigid projection remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The 17-source training mixture remains, but v2 substantially broadens evaluation to medical endoscopy, microscopy, additional cross-sensor registration and aerial temporal-map data through its cross-domain benchmark (Table 10). Appendix D.4 adds offline trajectory estimation on FusionPortablev2 and Newer College. ModelNet and TLS registration already appeared in v1 and are not wholly new coverage.

E2.justification: The pairwise comparison replaces Quatro with KISS-Matcher and adds previously absent NSS results for TEASER, BUFFER, PARENet and BUFFER-X. The new multi-view comparison evaluates RPF and a retrained BUFFER-X variant using RAP's training data. The SLAM comparison adds R3LIVE, FAST-LIO2, VINS-Fusion and DROID-SLAM. LMVR remains in v2's indoor comparison.

E3.justification: Reported training changes from two stages over seven days on eight A100 GPUs to three days and approximately 120k iterations on 32 A100s, with revised batching and a stated maximum of 16 rather than 24 training views. New evaluation protocols include scale-normalized edge/graph success thresholds, stricter thresholds, matched-data baseline training and SLAM sampling every 2 or 10 seconds.

E4.justification: v2 adds cross-domain analyses of overlap, view count, token-dependent runtime, stricter success thresholds and error distributions. Existing component ablations are extended to the new benchmark. However, v1 Table 10's extended integration-step, indoor-only-training and best-of-S studies disappear, as do its TLS tunnel/forest failure examples. The KITTI/Waymo distance analysis is retained in the appendix.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports empirical cumulative error distributions, overall and by scenario, in Figures 7–8. This adds distributional statistical reporting. Neither version supplies confidence intervals, significance tests or explicit repeated-training-run uncertainty; v1's multiple-generation selection budgets concern inference rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial cross-domain and SLAM results, including RAP's 85.9% edge and 77.3% graph success in Table 2. Retained results also change: 3DMatch pairwise success is 95.64% with S=5 in v1 Table 2 and 95.90% in v2 Table 1. Revised training and unspecified selection settings prevent treating this as a controlled performance gain. v1's comprehensive validation tables are removed.

T1.justification: The main flow equations, rigid projection, training loss and standard error formulas remain equivalent after renumbering. v1 Equation 8's explicit rigidity-residual definition is absent from v2. Appendix B.6 introduces definitions for edge/graph success and normalized global RMSE. Neither version contains a theorem or proof development.

C1.justification: v2 makes a newly proposed cross-domain benchmark a central contribution and claims leading zero-shot performance across its five categories in the abstract, introduction and conclusion. v1 instead emphasizes the registration model, rigidity-based sampling and selection, training recipe and existing benchmark performance. The separate generation-selection contribution is no longer claimed.

C2.justification: v2 interprets matched-data BUFFER-X results as evidence that data scaling alone cannot explain RAP's advantage, and adds explanations concerning pairwise-error propagation, global attention costs and implicit bundle adjustment. It introduces memory limits for very large view counts, while removing v1's explicit automotive real-time limitation and discussion of failures in unfamiliar TLS environments.

D1.justification: v2 adds inference defaults, baseline checkpoint/rescaling rules, benchmark source/license information and revised training details. It removes the explicit generation-selection procedure and budget, despite retaining a brief mention of selection. Reproducibility is complicated by conflicting learning rates: Section 4.1 gives 0.002/0.0002, whereas Appendix B.3 gives 0.005/0.0005; v1 consistently used the former.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands the cited registration literature, SLAM systems and cross-domain data sources. Section 2 newly positions RAP against virtual-correspondence approaches DeepVCP and DeepPRO, while Section 4.3 introduces the claimed absence of cross-domain evaluation as a research gap. These changes extend the positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract and contribution list are rewritten, and the experimental narrative is reorganized around separate pairwise and cross-domain multi-view sections. Earlier indoor comparisons and distance-based tests move into a restructured supplement with additional subsections. References are consolidated after the supplementary material instead of being interspersed with its figures and tables.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column layout. Figure 1 is redesigned, and v2 adds a benchmark infographic, robustness/runtime plots, ECDF panels and SLAM visualizations. Comparison tables are substantially restructured, while many earlier qualitative panels are retained, regrouped or relocated; the TLS failure panels are removed.

improvement.justification: The broader evaluation, matched-training-data BUFFER-X control and threshold/view-count analyses strengthen the empirical case beyond v1. These gains are tempered by unresolved support for the central zero-shot claim: nuScenes appears in both training Table 4 and benchmark Table 10 despite Section 4.3 claiming no dataset overlap. Conflicting learning rates and removal of several diagnostic ablations further limit reproducibility and transparency, making the net quality improvement modest.
